 N.C. approves new absentee ballot restrictions — right as mail-in ballots are issued
 The N.C. State Board of Elections voted along party lines to require officials to disqualify ballots with an unsealed envelope and limit who can drop off mail-in ballots. 
 James O’Hara , Senior Writer 
 • 
 September 7, 2026 
 Wren Silman Photo assets from Adobe Stock. 
 Friday morning, as North Carolina’s 100 county boards of elections began to send out mail-in ballots, the N.C. State Board of Elections changed how voters and counties must handle them. 
 Split across party lines, the State Board of Elections voted three to two — Republicans in approval and Democrats in dissent — to approve two numbered memos guiding counties on handling absentee ballots.  
 Among other changes, the memos redefine who can submit a completed absentee ballot, requiring counties to spoil and reissue absentee ballots when someone other than the voter, a close relative or legal guardian delivers them. 
 “Our concern, and it continues to be true, is that these types of guidance changes so close to when ballots are going out, which is today, would cause likely confusion for voters,” Sailor Jones, the North Carolina director of national watchdog organization Common Cause, said.   
 The absentee ballot changes were originally set to take effect on Jan. 1, 2027, after the N.C. General Assembly passed them into law in August. But the Board of Elections expedited this process, implementing the changes for the upcoming November midterms.  
 “So now we’re saying, ‘Oh yeah, well, we want to do it now, we want to do it anyway, we want to do it early,’” Siobhan O’Duffy Millen, a Democratic member of the board, said. “And maybe that’s okay, and maybe that’s getting a little ahead of ourselves. I can’t really answer that one.” 
 The memos also changed how counties handle unsealed absentee ballots and the submission of multiple ballots in one envelope. Counties are now instructed to spoil an absentee ballot when its return envelope contains more than one ballot — or if a ballot arrives in an unsealed container envelope.  
 Deanna De’Liberto, the second vice chairwoman of the Guilford County Republican Party, said multiple ballots occasionally come in the same ballot return envelope. 
 “Sometimes your husband and wife will get their ballots around at the same time and a ballot will be returned in the wrong return envelope,” she said. “And so the question is, do you count that ballot?” 
 Now, the answer is no. In the upcoming election, ballots with these errors will be spoiled and will not count.  
 “Previously, we would say, well, ‘They sealed the outer envelope, they signed everything, they had a witness or a notary. So just because they didn’t lick an envelope, we shouldn’t throw out their vote,’” Millen said.  
 The Board of Elections originally met on Sept. 2 to discuss the memos, but sent the meeting to recess, reconvening on Friday at 9 a.m. The board made the numbered memos publicly available less than two hours before the Friday meeting. 
 The decision to provide numbered memo guidance follows a set of election rules the board passed earlier this year, which are currently subject to legislative review after receiving letters of objection and will not have any effect on the midterms.  
 Among the rules were the changes made in the numbered memos, restrictions on noise in areas surrounding voting sites, recounts and photo ID exemptions.  
 After the Board of Elections passed the rules in July, they were subject to review by the N.C. Rules Review Commission.  
 Jake Parker, the chair of the commission, said the commission is limited to considering if the agency has the authority to adopt a rule, if the rule is clear and unambiguous and if the agency followed the rulemaking process in its review. 
 “Our personal opinions are put aside with respect to whether the agency’s policy actually makes sense or whether we would agree with it,” Parker said. “That does not come into our analysis.” 
 On Aug. 27, the commission approved the new rules.  
 Following commission approval, rule changes may be subject to legislative review by the N.C. General Assembly if the Rules Review Commission receives 10 or more letters of objection by 5 p.m. the day after a rule is approved.  
 The Commission received 714 pages of letters of objection and sent the rules to legislative review. 
 Despite this, the board provided numbered memo guidance, implementing the rule changes on absentee ballots anyway.  
 “We have the statutory authority to act by numbered memo, as this board well knows and has done many a time,” Stacy “Four” Eggers, a Republican board member, said during Friday’s meeting.  
 But other advocates disagree, as Jones said the board acted despite voters’ objections to the formal rules.  
 “We think this is a real violation of the public trust and will result in eligible ballots being spoiled during what we all know is a real high-interest midterm election,” Jones said. 
 Millen said that while the new memos are binding, some county board members view them as just guidance.  
 “My feeling on numbered memos is that people treat them as law and they’re not really law,” De’Liberto said. “And so in the past, numbered memos have really been interpretations of the statute, and sometimes they get it wrong.” 
 Regardless of the changes, Jones said voters should not be deterred from voting.  
 “If you’re questioning whether your vote matters in 2026, there’s no better evidence than last-minute changes by terrified politicians meant to trick you into thinking it’s not worth it,” Jones wrote in a statement to The Daily Tar Heel.
